props.title: Evil Roy Slade

sections.content: Evil Roy Slade stands as a brilliant but overlooked Western comedy that perfectly satirizes the genre's tropes. Coming at a time when traditional Westerns like The Cowboys (1972) were still being made seriously, this TV movie written by Garry Marshall and Jerry Belson gleefully skewers every Western cliché. John Astin's performance as the titular character - a man so evil he was raised by coyotes - channels the manic energy of Blazing Saddles (1974) two years before Mel Brooks tackled the genre.

sections.content: The film's genius lies in its commitment to absurdist humor while maintaining Western aesthetics. Like ¡Three Amigos! (1986) would later perfect, Evil Roy Slade understands that the best genre parodies come from loving the source material. Mickey Rooney's performance as the vengeful railroad magnate Nelson L. Stool follows in the grand tradition of pompous Western villains, while Dick Shawn's psychiatrist character Dr. Lovecraft predates City Slickers (1991) urban-meets-frontier comedy by nearly 20 years.

The made-for-TV origins actually worked in the film's favor, allowing for a more episodic structure that plays like a series of interconnected comedy sketches. This format influenced later Western comedies like Rustlers' Rhapsody (1985) and Back to the Future Part III (1990), proving that the genre's tropes were ripe for satire while still maintaining audience appeal. sections.content: While not as widely known as Blazing Saddles (1974), Evil Roy Slade helped establish many of the Western comedy conventions that would become standard. The film's influence can be seen in everything from The Frisco Kid (1979) to modern takes like A Million Ways to Die in the West (2014). Its particular blend of slapstick and character-driven humor created a template for how to successfully merge comedy with Western traditions.
